fm_projectiles_components.description: Use common time for horizontal and vertical motion, and choose physical time roots for projectile events.

sections.title: How do horizontal and vertical motion differ?
sections.label: Resolve the motion
sections.intro: In the particle model there is only a constant downward gravitational acceleration. The model neglects air resistance, spin and finite size. Use the same clock for both axes.

blocks.html: Take up as positive. With launch components \(u_x,u_y\), use \(x=u_xt\), \(y=u_yt-\frac12gt^2\), \(v_x=u_x\) and \(v_y=u_y-gt\).

blocks.title: Use the same time in two directions
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(17\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the horizontal and vertical displacements after \(1\,\mathrm s\).

retry.feedback: Include the contribution from vertical acceleration.

blocks.hint: Use one shared time, with different accelerations along the axes.
blocks.solution:
Choose right and up positive. The horizontal acceleration is zero and the vertical acceleration is \(-g\).

At the stated time, \(x=10\times 1=10\).

Vertically, \(y=17\times 1-5\left(1\right)^2=12\). The two displacements are \(10\,\mathrm m\) and \(12\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Adding a horizontal gravity term invents a force in that direction.

sections.title: What stops changing sign at the highest point?
sections.label: Find maximum height
sections.intro: As the particle rises, \(v_y\) is positive. It becomes negative once the particle starts descending.

blocks.html: Set \(v_y=0\) to find the time of maximum height. The horizontal component need not vanish.

figure.alt: A parabolic path rises to H, and the tangent there points horizontally.
figure.caption: At the apex the horizontal motion continues, even though \(v_y=0\).

blocks.title: Find the highest point
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time and the maximum height above the launch point.

retry.feedback: The apex is midway through flight only when the endpoint returns to launch level. The requested time is to the apex.

blocks.hint: At the top only the vertical component is zero.
blocks.solution:
At the top the vertical velocity satisfies \(v_y=16-10t=0\).

\(t=\frac{8}{5}\) seconds. The horizontal velocity remains \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Substitute this time into the vertical displacement, giving the maximum height \(\frac{64}{5}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Do not set the full speed to zero at the apex.

sections.title: Which crossing does the question mean?
sections.label: Choose the event time
sections.intro: A specified height may be crossed twice. Find both possibilities on the flight interval and check whether the vertical velocity is positive or negative.

blocks.html: Use \(v_y=u_y-gt\) to distinguish rising and falling. A positive root may still lie beyond the first contact.

blocks.title: Choose the descending event
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(\frac{35}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At what time does it cross height \(\frac{25}{2}\,\mathrm m\) above launch while descending? Find its horizontal distance at that time too.

retry.feedback: That is the earlier crossing. At that time the vertical component is positive.

blocks.hint: Two roots can both be physically real. Select the one with the requested velocity sign.
blocks.solution:
Set the vertical displacement equal to the stated height: \(- 5 t^{2} + \frac{35 t}{2}=\frac{25}{2}\).

The two times are \(1\,\mathrm s\) and \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\). The vertical velocity at the later time is negative.

The descending time is \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\). Constant horizontal velocity places it \(30\,\mathrm m\) from launch horizontally.

blocks.html: An earlier crossing is not a falling crossing just because the projectile eventually lands.

blocks.title: Choose the descending event
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(\frac{55}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At what time does it cross height \(35\,\mathrm m\) above launch while descending? Find its horizontal distance at that time too.

retry.feedback: That is the earlier crossing. At that time the vertical component is positive.

blocks.hint: Two roots can both be physically real. Select the one with the requested velocity sign.
blocks.solution:
Set the vertical displacement equal to the stated height: \(- 5 t^{2} + \frac{55 t}{2}=35\).

The two times are \(2\,\mathrm s\) and \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\). The vertical velocity at the later time is negative.

The descending time is \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\). Constant horizontal velocity places it \(63\,\mathrm m\) from launch horizontally.

sections.title: How do I find the direction while descending?
sections.label: Recombine velocity
sections.intro: Velocity components are signed. The speed uses their squared magnitudes. The direction needs both a reference axis and which side of that axis the motion points.

blocks.html: With \(v_x>0\) and \(v_y<0\), speed is \(\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\) and the angle below horizontal has tangent \(\frac{|v_y|}{v_x}\).

blocks.title: Find the direction of motion from the components
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(17\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact speed and the tangent of its angle below the horizontal after \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\).

retry.feedback: The direction is already stated as below the horizontal. Its acute angle has positive tangent.

blocks.hint: Use the velocity components at the requested time, not the launch angle.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal velocity is \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the signed vertical velocity is \(-8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Combine perpendicular components using Pythagoras. Speed is \(2 \sqrt{65}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The direction is below the horizontal, with tangent \(\frac{4}{7}\). The speed is \(2 \sqrt{65}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: The initial launch angle does not stay constant.

sections.title: How do I find time of flight and range?
sections.label: Find the landing
sections.intro: Use the landing height in the vertical equation. If launch and landing are at the same level with \(u_y>0\), then the non-zero flight time is \(\frac{2u_y}{g}\).

blocks.html: For an elevated launch use the actual negative vertical displacement. Then use \(x=u_xt\) with the physical impact time.

blocks.title: Find the range on level ground
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). It lands back on the same horizontal level. Find the time of flight and range.

retry.feedback: Zero is the launch time. Use the later root.

blocks.hint: Solve for the positive time at zero vertical displacement. Then apply the horizontal equation.
blocks.solution:
Return to the launch level gives \(- 5 t^{2} + 13 t=0\).

Factor out time. Zero is the launch time, so the landing time is \(\frac{13}{5}\,\mathrm s\).

Time of flight is \(\frac{13}{5}\,\mathrm s\) and the horizontal range is \(26\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: The level-ground range formula does not apply to a landing below the launch point.

blocks.title: Find the range on level ground
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(17\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). It lands back on the same horizontal level. Find the time of flight and range.

retry.feedback: Zero is the launch time. Use the later root.

blocks.hint: Solve for the positive time at zero vertical displacement. Then apply the horizontal equation.
blocks.solution:
Return to the launch level gives \(- 5 t^{2} + 17 t=0\).

Factor out time. Zero is the launch time, so the landing time is \(\frac{17}{5}\,\mathrm s\).

Time of flight is \(\frac{17}{5}\,\mathrm s\) and the horizontal range is \(\frac{238}{5}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Use the same time in two directions
examples.question: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the horizontal and vertical displacements after \(\frac{2}{3}\,\mathrm s\).
solution: Choose right and up positive. The horizontal acceleration is zero and the vertical acceleration is \(-g\).
At the stated time, \(x=8\times \frac{2}{3}=\frac{16}{3}\).
Vertically, \(y=14\times \frac{2}{3}-5\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2=\frac{64}{9}\). The two displacements are \(\frac{16}{3}\,\mathrm m\) and \(\frac{64}{9}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Find the highest point
examples.question: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time and the maximum height above the launch point.
solution: At the top the vertical velocity satisfies \(v_y=13-10t=0\).
\(t=\frac{13}{10}\) seconds. The horizontal velocity remains \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Substitute this time into the vertical displacement, giving the maximum height \(\frac{169}{20}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Choose the descending event
examples.question: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(\frac{25}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At what time does it cross height \(5\,\mathrm m\) above launch while descending? Find its horizontal distance at that time too.
solution: Set the vertical displacement equal to the stated height: \(- 5 t^{2} + \frac{25 t}{2}=5\).
The two times are \(\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and \(2\,\mathrm s\). The vertical velocity at the later time is negative.
The descending time is \(2\,\mathrm s\). Constant horizontal velocity places it \(18\,\mathrm m\) from launch horizontally.

examples.title: Choose the descending event
examples.question: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(\frac{45}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At what time does it cross height \(\frac{45}{2}\,\mathrm m\) above launch while descending? Find its horizontal distance at that time too.
solution: Set the vertical displacement equal to the stated height: \(- 5 t^{2} + \frac{45 t}{2}=\frac{45}{2}\).
The two times are \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and \(3\,\mathrm s\). The vertical velocity at the later time is negative.
The descending time is \(3\,\mathrm s\). Constant horizontal velocity places it \(45\,\mathrm m\) from launch horizontally.

examples.title: Find the direction of motion from the components
examples.question: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact speed and the tangent of its angle below the horizontal after \(2\,\mathrm s\).
solution: The horizontal velocity is \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the signed vertical velocity is \(-4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Combine perpendicular components using Pythagoras. Speed is \(4 \sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
The direction is below the horizontal, with tangent \(\frac{1}{3}\). The speed is \(4 \sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Land below a horizontal launch
examples.question: A practice ball leaves a ledge horizontally at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The ground is \(\frac{45}{4}\,\mathrm m\) below the ledge. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its first impact time and horizontal distance.
solution: The upwards velocity starts at zero. In the vertical equation use \(y=- \frac{45}{4}\).
So \(5t^2=\frac{45}{4}\) gives \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\) after launch. The negative root is outside the flight interval.
The time to the ground is \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and the horizontal distance is \(15\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Land below a horizontal launch
examples.question: A practice ball leaves a ledge horizontally at \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The ground is \(\frac{125}{4}\,\mathrm m\) below the ledge. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its first impact time and horizontal distance.
solution: The upwards velocity starts at zero. In the vertical equation use \(y=- \frac{125}{4}\).
So \(5t^2=\frac{125}{4}\) gives \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\) after launch. The negative root is outside the flight interval.
The time to the ground is \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and the horizontal distance is \(35\,\mathrm m\).

extraPractice.title: Use the same time in two directions
extraPractice.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the horizontal and vertical displacements after \(\frac{4}{3}\,\mathrm s\).

Vertically, \(y=20\times \frac{4}{3}-5\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2=\frac{160}{9}\). The two displacements are \(16\,\mathrm m\) and \(\frac{160}{9}\,\mathrm m\).

extraPractice.title: Find the highest point
extraPractice.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(19\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time and the maximum height above the launch point.

retry.feedback: The apex is midway through flight only when the endpoint returns to launch level. The requested time is to the apex.

extraPractice.solution:
At the top the vertical velocity satisfies \(v_y=19-10t=0\).

\(t=\frac{19}{10}\) seconds. The horizontal velocity remains \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Substitute this time into the vertical displacement, giving the maximum height \(\frac{361}{20}\,\mathrm m\).

extraPractice.title: Choose the descending event
extraPractice.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(\frac{65}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At what time does it cross height \(50\,\mathrm m\) above launch while descending? Find its horizontal distance at that time too.

retry.feedback: That is the earlier crossing. At that time the vertical component is positive.

extraPractice.hint: Two roots can both be physically real. Select the one with the requested velocity sign.
extraPractice.solution:
Set the vertical displacement equal to the stated height: \(- 5 t^{2} + \frac{65 t}{2}=50\).

The two times are \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and \(4\,\mathrm s\). The vertical velocity at the later time is negative.

The descending time is \(4\,\mathrm s\). Constant horizontal velocity places it \(84\,\mathrm m\) from launch horizontally.

extraPractice.title: Find the direction of motion from the components
extraPractice.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact speed and the tangent of its angle below the horizontal after \(3\,\mathrm s\).

retry.feedback: The direction is already stated as below the horizontal. Its acute angle has positive tangent.

extraPractice.hint: Use the velocity components at the requested time, not the launch angle.
extraPractice.solution:
The horizontal velocity is \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the signed vertical velocity is \(-12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Combine perpendicular components using Pythagoras. Speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The direction is below the horizontal, with tangent \(\frac{3}{4}\). The speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

extraPractice.title: Land below a horizontal launch
extraPractice.prompt: A practice ball leaves a ledge horizontally at \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The ground is \(\frac{245}{4}\,\mathrm m\) below the ledge. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its first impact time and horizontal distance.

retry.feedback: A negative time is outside the post-launch flight.

extraPractice.hint: Find the time from the vertical drop, then use constant horizontal velocity.
extraPractice.solution:
The upwards velocity starts at zero. In the vertical equation use \(y=- \frac{245}{4}\).

So \(5t^2=\frac{245}{4}\) gives \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\) after launch. The negative root is outside the flight interval.

The time to the ground is \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\) and the horizontal distance is \(63\,\mathrm m\).

glossary.definition: The horizontal displacement from launch to landing.
The signed part measured along one axis.

revision.body:
Choose the next step

SituationMethod
Horizontal\(x=u_xt\) and \(v_x=u_x\).
Vertical\(y=u_yt-\frac12gt^2\) and \(v_y=u_y-gt\).
Highest pointUse \(v_y=0\), then find \(y\).
ImpactUse the required landing height and check the physical root.

Try a quick check

For \(u_x=8,\ u_y=15,\ g=10\) in SI units, find the level-ground range.

Check The non-zero time is \(3\,\mathrm s\), so the range is \(24\,\mathrm m\).
revision.checks:
• Adding a horizontal gravity term invents a force in that direction.
  • Do not set the full speed to zero at the apex.
revision.examTip: Write a shared time before substituting into both axes.

fm_projectiles_trajectories.description: Eliminate time, recover unknown launch settings and use a trajectory to decide clearance and impact positions.

sections.title: How do I turn two time equations into one path?
sections.label: Eliminate time
sections.intro: The two component equations describe a position at a given time. To describe the path directly, eliminate time using the simpler horizontal equation.

blocks.html: For non-zero \(u_x\), \(t=\frac{x}{u_x}\) gives \(y=\frac{u_y}{u_x}x-\frac{g}{2u_x^2}x^2\), relative to launch.

blocks.title: Eliminate time to find a Cartesian trajectory
blocks.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Write the trajectory as \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). Find \(A\) and \(C\).

retry.feedback: The formula already subtracts the quadratic term. C itself is positive.

blocks.hint: The horizontal equation is easiest to rearrange for time when the horizontal speed is non-zero.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal equation gives \(t=\frac{x}{9}\).

Substitute for time in \(y=- 5 t^{2} + 20 t\). This gives \(y=- \frac{5 x^{2}}{81} + \frac{20 x}{9}\).

Thus \(A=\frac{20}{9}\) and \(C=\frac{5}{81}\).

blocks.html: The coordinate equation describes the path only on the physically valid flight stage.

sections.title: What do the trajectory coefficients tell me about launch?
sections.label: Read the coefficients
sections.intro: The initial slope is the tangent of the launch angle for a rightward launch. The curvature coefficient also depends on horizontal speed, so the two coefficients together determine both components.

blocks.html: Read \(C=\frac{g}{2u_x^2}\) and \(A=\frac{u_y}{u_x}\) in \(y=Ax-Cx^2\).

blocks.title: Recover the launch from its trajectory
blocks.prompt: A right-moving practice ball follows \(y=- \frac{5 x^{2}}{256} + \frac{11 x}{16}\), with coordinates measured from launch. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact launch speed and the tangent of its launch angle above the horizontal.

retry.feedback: The horizontal speed is one component of the launch velocity. Use both components.

blocks.hint: Identify the quadratic coefficient to recover the horizontal speed, then use the slope at launch.
blocks.solution:
The quadratic coefficient in magnitude is \(\frac{g}{2u_x^2}\). Taking the positive square root gives horizontal speed \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The linear coefficient is \(\frac{u_y}{u_x}\), so the vertical component is \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The exact launch speed is \(\sqrt{377}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the tangent of the angle is \(\frac{11}{16}\).

blocks.html: The horizontal component by itself is not the launch speed unless the vertical component is zero.

sections.title: How do I find the trajectory from two measured positions?
sections.label: Use two independent points
sections.intro: When launch is the origin, the constant term is already known. Two distinct non-zero horizontal coordinates let you solve for the other two coefficients.

blocks.html: At each observed point, divide by its non-zero \(x\)-coordinate to obtain \(\frac yx=A-Cx\).

blocks.title: Find an unknown trajectory from two positions
blocks.prompt: The trajectory from the origin is \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). In metre coordinates its path passes through \((4,\frac{44}{9})\) and \((8,\frac{56}{9})\). Find both coefficients.
blocks.hint: After dividing each equation by its x-coordinate, subtract to eliminate A.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the coordinates of each point. This gives two linear equations in the unknown coefficients.

Divide each fitted equation by its non-zero horizontal coordinate. The reduced equations are \(A - 4 C=\frac{11}{9}\) and \(A - 8 C=\frac{7}{9}\).

Subtract to find \(C=\frac{1}{9}\), then substitute to find \(A=\frac{5}{3}\).

blocks.html: The launch point alone does not constrain either coefficient beyond the known zero intercept.

blocks.title: Find an unknown trajectory from two positions
blocks.prompt: The trajectory from the origin is \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). In metre coordinates its path passes through \((6,\frac{118}{11})\) and \((10,\frac{470}{33})\). Find both coefficients.
blocks.hint: After dividing each equation by its x-coordinate, subtract to eliminate A.
blocks.solution:
Substitute the coordinates of each point. This gives two linear equations in the unknown coefficients.

Divide each fitted equation by its non-zero horizontal coordinate. The reduced equations are \(A - 6 C=\frac{59}{33}\) and \(A - 10 C=\frac{47}{33}\).

Subtract to find \(C=\frac{1}{11}\), then substitute to find \(A=\frac{7}{3}\).

sections.title: Over which positions is the ball high enough?
sections.label: Solve a height inequality
sections.intro: A level reference line can cut the trajectory at two positions. Find the intersection points, then check where the path lies above the line.

blocks.html: For ‘at least’, solve \(y(x)-h\ge0\), include equality, and restrict to the physical flight.

figure.alt: The path crosses a fixed height line at two positions x₁ and x₂.
figure.caption: A height clearance applies between the two intersections. Whether the endpoints count depends on the wording.

blocks.title: Find the full interval clearing a height line
blocks.prompt: The height above level ground is \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{8} + \frac{15 x}{8}\). On the flight, find the inclusive interval of horizontal positions where the height is at least \(\frac{9}{2}\,\mathrm m\). Enter its two endpoints.
blocks.hint: Solve the equality first, then determine the sign between the roots. At least includes equality.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the required height from the trajectory. The clearance inequality factors as \(\left(\frac{3}{8} - \frac{x}{8}\right) \left(x - 12\right)\ge0\).

The downward-opening parabola is at or above the line between its two intersections, including the endpoints.

The interval is \(3\le x\le 12\). Both endpoints are inside the physical flight.

blocks.html: The roots delimit the interval. The answer is not just the two roots.

sections.title: How does a sloping landing change the equation?
sections.label: Match both heights
sections.intro: At landing, the projectile and the slope have the same vertical coordinate at the same horizontal coordinate.

blocks.html: Set \(y_{\rm path}(x)=y_{\rm slope}(x)\), then take the first physical point after launch.

blocks.title: Intersect the trajectory with rising ground
blocks.prompt: A projected ball has trajectory \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{13} + \frac{5 x}{3}\) from the origin. A slope through launch has equation \(y=\frac{x}{2}\). Find the non-zero horizontal displacement where the ball meets the slope and the height there.

retry.feedback: This is the level-ground root. Set the trajectory equal to the height of the slope.

blocks.hint: For an inclined ground line the endpoint need not have zero vertical displacement.
blocks.solution:
Set the two height equations equal rather than using a level-ground range.

Factor out \(x\). The zero root describes launch. The other solution is \(x=\frac{91}{6}\).

The impact is at horizontal distance \(\frac{91}{6}\,\mathrm m\) and height \(\frac{91}{12}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Returning to launch height and meeting a sloped line are different events.

blocks.title: Intersect the trajectory with rising ground
blocks.prompt: A projected ball has trajectory \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{15} + \frac{7 x}{3}\) from the origin. A slope through launch has equation \(y=x\). Find the non-zero horizontal displacement where the ball meets the slope and the height there.

retry.feedback: This is the level-ground root. Set the trajectory equal to the height of the slope.

blocks.hint: For an inclined ground line the endpoint need not have zero vertical displacement.
blocks.solution:
Set the two height equations equal rather than using a level-ground range.

Factor out \(x\). The zero root describes launch. The other solution is \(x=20\).

The impact is at horizontal distance \(20\,\mathrm m\) and height \(20\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Eliminate time to find a Cartesian trajectory
examples.question: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(17\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Write the trajectory as \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). Find \(A\) and \(C\).
solution: The horizontal equation gives \(t=\frac{x}{7}\).
Substitute for time in \(y=- 5 t^{2} + 17 t\). This gives \(y=- \frac{5 x^{2}}{49} + \frac{17 x}{7}\).

examples.title: Recover the launch from its trajectory
examples.question: A right-moving practice ball follows \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{45} + \frac{3 x}{5}\), with coordinates measured from launch. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact launch speed and the tangent of its launch angle above the horizontal.
solution: The quadratic coefficient in magnitude is \(\frac{g}{2u_x^2}\). Taking the positive square root gives horizontal speed \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
The linear coefficient is \(\frac{u_y}{u_x}\), so the vertical component is \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
The exact launch speed is \(3 \sqrt{34}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the tangent of the angle is \(\frac{3}{5}\).

examples.title: Find an unknown trajectory from two positions
examples.question: The trajectory from the origin is \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). In metre coordinates its path passes through \((3,\frac{23}{8})\) and \((7,\frac{77}{24})\). Find both coefficients.
solution: Substitute the coordinates of each point. This gives two linear equations in the unknown coefficients.
Divide each fitted equation by its non-zero horizontal coordinate. The reduced equations are \(A - 3 C=\frac{23}{24}\) and \(A - 7 C=\frac{11}{24}\).
Subtract to find \(C=\frac{1}{8}\), then substitute to find \(A=\frac{4}{3}\).

examples.title: Find an unknown trajectory from two positions
examples.question: The trajectory from the origin is \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). In metre coordinates its path passes through \((5,\frac{15}{2})\) and \((9,\frac{99}{10})\). Find both coefficients.
solution: Substitute the coordinates of each point. This gives two linear equations in the unknown coefficients.
Divide each fitted equation by its non-zero horizontal coordinate. The reduced equations are \(A - 5 C=\frac{3}{2}\) and \(A - 9 C=\frac{11}{10}\).
Subtract to find \(C=\frac{1}{10}\), then substitute to find \(A=2\).

examples.title: Find the full interval clearing a height line
examples.question: The height above level ground is \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{7} + \frac{11 x}{7}\). On the flight, find the inclusive interval of horizontal positions where the height is at least \(\frac{18}{7}\,\mathrm m\). Enter its two endpoints.
solution: Subtract the required height from the trajectory. The clearance inequality factors as \(\left(\frac{2}{7} - \frac{x}{7}\right) \left(x - 9\right)\ge0\).
The downward-opening parabola is at or above the line between its two intersections, including the endpoints.
The interval is \(2\le x\le 9\). Both endpoints are inside the physical flight.

examples.title: Intersect the trajectory with rising ground
examples.question: A projected ball has trajectory \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{12} + \frac{4 x}{3}\) from the origin. A slope through launch has equation \(y=\frac{x}{4}\). Find the non-zero horizontal displacement where the ball meets the slope and the height there.
solution: Set the two height equations equal rather than using a level-ground range.
Factor out \(x\). The zero root describes launch. The other solution is \(x=13\).
The impact is at horizontal distance \(13\,\mathrm m\) and height \(\frac{13}{4}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Intersect the trajectory with rising ground
examples.question: A projected ball has trajectory \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{14} + 2 x\) from the origin. A slope through launch has equation \(y=\frac{3 x}{4}\). Find the non-zero horizontal displacement where the ball meets the slope and the height there.
solution: Set the two height equations equal rather than using a level-ground range.
Factor out \(x\). The zero root describes launch. The other solution is \(x=\frac{35}{2}\).
The impact is at horizontal distance \(\frac{35}{2}\,\mathrm m\) and height \(\frac{105}{8}\,\mathrm m\).

extraPractice.title: Eliminate time to find a Cartesian trajectory
extraPractice.prompt: A practice ball is projected with horizontal velocity \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards velocity \(23\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Write the trajectory as \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). Find \(A\) and \(C\).

retry.feedback: The formula already subtracts the quadratic term. C itself is positive.

extraPractice.hint: The horizontal equation is easiest to rearrange for time when the horizontal speed is non-zero.
extraPractice.solution:
The horizontal equation gives \(t=\frac{x}{11}\).

Substitute for time in \(y=- 5 t^{2} + 23 t\). This gives \(y=- \frac{5 x^{2}}{121} + \frac{23 x}{11}\).

Thus \(A=\frac{23}{11}\) and \(C=\frac{5}{121}\).

extraPractice.title: Recover the launch from its trajectory
extraPractice.prompt: A right-moving practice ball follows \(y=- \frac{5 x^{2}}{289} + \frac{13 x}{17}\), with coordinates measured from launch. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact launch speed and the tangent of its launch angle above the horizontal.

retry.feedback: The horizontal speed is one component of the launch velocity. Use both components.

extraPractice.hint: Identify the quadratic coefficient to recover the horizontal speed, then use the slope at launch.
extraPractice.solution:
The quadratic coefficient in magnitude is \(\frac{g}{2u_x^2}\). Taking the positive square root gives horizontal speed \(17\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The linear coefficient is \(\frac{u_y}{u_x}\), so the vertical component is \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The exact launch speed is \(\sqrt{458}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the tangent of the angle is \(\frac{13}{17}\).

extraPractice.title: Find an unknown trajectory from two positions
extraPractice.prompt: The trajectory from the origin is \(y=Ax-Cx^2\). In metre coordinates its path passes through \((7,\frac{175}{12})\) and \((11,\frac{77}{4})\). Find both coefficients.
extraPractice.hint: After dividing each equation by its x-coordinate, subtract to eliminate A.
extraPractice.solution:
Substitute the coordinates of each point. This gives two linear equations in the unknown coefficients.

Divide each fitted equation by its non-zero horizontal coordinate. The reduced equations are \(A - 7 C=\frac{25}{12}\) and \(A - 11 C=\frac{7}{4}\).

Subtract to find \(C=\frac{1}{12}\), then substitute to find \(A=\frac{8}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Find the full interval clearing a height line
extraPractice.prompt: The height above level ground is \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{19 x}{9}\). On the flight, find the inclusive interval of horizontal positions where the height is at least \(\frac{20}{3}\,\mathrm m\). Enter its two endpoints.
extraPractice.hint: Solve the equality first, then determine the sign between the roots. At least includes equality.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract the required height from the trajectory. The clearance inequality factors as \(\left(\frac{4}{9} - \frac{x}{9}\right) \left(x - 15\right)\ge0\).

The downward-opening parabola is at or above the line between its two intersections, including the endpoints.

The interval is \(4\le x\le 15\). Both endpoints are inside the physical flight.

extraPractice.title: Intersect the trajectory with rising ground
extraPractice.prompt: A projected ball has trajectory \(y=- \frac{x^{2}}{16} + \frac{8 x}{3}\) from the origin. A slope through launch has equation \(y=\frac{5 x}{4}\). Find the non-zero horizontal displacement where the ball meets the slope and the height there.

retry.feedback: This is the level-ground root. Set the trajectory equal to the height of the slope.

extraPractice.hint: For an inclined ground line the endpoint need not have zero vertical displacement.
extraPractice.solution:
Set the two height equations equal rather than using a level-ground range.

Factor out \(x\). The zero root describes launch. The other solution is \(x=\frac{68}{3}\).

The impact is at horizontal distance \(\frac{68}{3}\,\mathrm m\) and height \(\frac{85}{3}\,\mathrm m\).

glossary.definition: The amount by which the projectile lies above a stated height.

• The coordinate equation describes the path only on the physically valid flight stage.
  • The horizontal component by itself is not the launch speed unless the vertical component is zero.
revision.examTip: Use a clear origin, especially when the given heights are measured from different levels.

related.title: Meetings, rebounds and release into free flight

fm_projectiles_stages.description: Synchronise meeting events, start a new stage after contact or release, and check the first physical event.

sections.title: What does it mean for two projectiles to meet?
sections.label: Use one common clock
sections.intro: Equal height alone is insufficient. Compare both position coordinates on a clock common to the two balls.

blocks.html: For simultaneous launches, use the same elapsed time \(t\) in both flights and test both coordinate equations.

blocks.title: Synchronise two airborne balls
blocks.prompt: Ball A is thrown right from the origin with initial horizontal and upwards velocity components \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Ball B begins at the same time and level \(6\,\mathrm m\) to the right, with initial components \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time from A's launch to their meeting and its height above launch.
blocks.hint: For a meeting both coordinates must agree at one clock time.
blocks.solution:
Use clock time \(t\) for A and \(t\) for B.

Equating horizontal positions gives \(7 t=4 t + 6\), so \(t=2\). At this time both balls have been launched.

Substitute each ball's own elapsed time into its vertical equation. Both heights equal \(22\,\mathrm m\). The meeting occurs \(2\,\mathrm s\) after A launches.

blocks.html: Identical horizontal positions can occur while the objects remain vertically separated.

sections.title: How does a delayed launch change the equations?
sections.label: Use the correct elapsed times
sections.intro: If the second launch occurs \(d\) seconds later, a common time \(t\) from the first launch corresponds to \(t-d\) for the second.

blocks.html: Check \(t\ge d\) before using the second ball's flight formula. Substitute the two elapsed times into their own vertical equations.

blocks.title: Synchronise two airborne balls
blocks.prompt: Ball A is thrown right from the origin with initial horizontal and upwards velocity components \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Ball B is thrown right from the same origin \(1\,\mathrm s\) later with components \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(27\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time from A's launch to their meeting and its height above launch.

retry.feedback: That is the time from B's launch. Use the common clock starting with A.

blocks.hint: For a meeting both coordinates must agree at one clock time.
blocks.solution:
Use clock time \(t\) for A and \(t-1\) for B.

Equating horizontal positions gives \(7 t=14 t - 14\), so \(t=2\). At this time both balls have been launched.

Substitute each ball's own elapsed time into its vertical equation. Both heights equal \(22\,\mathrm m\). The meeting occurs \(2\,\mathrm s\) after A launches.

blocks.html: Substituting one elapsed time into both models ignores the launch delay.

sections.title: What carries over into a rebound on a smooth floor?
sections.label: Restart the flight
sections.intro: A smooth horizontal floor changes only the vertical velocity during the impact. The ball starts the second flight at the contact point.

blocks.html: With coefficient of restitution \(e\), the upward component after impact equals \(e\) times the incoming downward speed.

figure.alt: A descending arc reaches B on the ground, then a rising arc leads to the next landing.
figure.caption: Use the velocity immediately after the bounce to begin the second free-flight calculation.

blocks.title: Start a new stage after a smooth-floor bounce
blocks.prompt: A ball meets a fixed smooth horizontal floor with horizontal speed \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and downwards speed \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The coefficient of restitution is \(\frac{4}{9}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its upwards speed immediately after the bounce and horizontal distance to its next landing on the floor.

retry.feedback: The rebound has positive vertical velocity because the floor impulse has reversed it.

blocks.hint: Apply restitution to the vertical component only. Then use ordinary projectile motion with the new initial velocity.
blocks.solution:
The floor impulse is vertical. The horizontal component remains unchanged, and restitution gives upwards component \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Restart time at the bounce. The condition \(- 5 t^{2} + 8 t=0\) has a non-zero solution \(\frac{8}{5}\,\mathrm s\).

The upwards speed after impact is \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the horizontal distance in the second flight is \(\frac{88}{5}\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: Do not multiply the whole velocity or the horizontal component by the coefficient of restitution.

blocks.title: Start a new stage after a smooth-floor bounce
blocks.prompt: A ball meets a fixed smooth horizontal floor with horizontal speed \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and downwards speed \(24\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The coefficient of restitution is \(\frac{2}{3}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its upwards speed immediately after the bounce and horizontal distance to its next landing on the floor.

retry.feedback: The rebound has positive vertical velocity because the floor impulse has reversed it.

blocks.hint: Apply restitution to the vertical component only. Then use ordinary projectile motion with the new initial velocity.
blocks.solution:
The floor impulse is vertical. The horizontal component remains unchanged, and restitution gives upwards component \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Restart time at the bounce. The condition \(- 5 t^{2} + 16 t=0\) has a non-zero solution \(\frac{16}{5}\,\mathrm s\).

The upwards speed after impact is \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the horizontal distance in the second flight is \(48\,\mathrm m\).

sections.title: Which initial velocity is used after release?
sections.label: Use the tangent at release
sections.intro: A smooth guide can steer an object before it is released. Its launch position and the tangent velocity at release become the starting data for free flight.

blocks.html: Use a local clock beginning at release. Gravity acts vertically after release, and the horizontal component then stays constant.

blocks.title: Use the tangent velocity at release
blocks.prompt: A ball leaves a guide with speed \(2 \sqrt{41}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The tangent direction at release is right and upwards with tangent \(\frac{4}{5}\). The ball then moves freely. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the horizontal and vertical displacements \(2\,\mathrm s\) after it leaves the guide.
blocks.hint: Start a fresh clock at the instant the ball leaves the guide. Use its tangent, not an old direction within the guide.
blocks.solution:
The free-flight initial velocity is the tangent velocity at release. Its rightwards and upwards components are \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Once free, the ball’s horizontal velocity is constant and its vertical acceleration is \(-g\).

The rightwards displacement is \(20\,\mathrm m\) and the signed upwards displacement is \(-4\,\mathrm m\).

blocks.html: An acceleration formula for the guide is no longer the flight model after release.

sections.title: How do I find which contact happens first?
sections.label: Choose the earliest valid time
sections.intro: Find candidate times for each boundary while assuming free flight. Reject those that are negative or occur after another boundary is reached.

blocks.html: The earliest valid contact ends the current stage. A root of a later hypothetical event is not part of that flight.

blocks.title: Compare two candidate first events
blocks.prompt: A ball is launched \(\frac{75}{4}\,\mathrm m\) above horizontal ground with rightwards speed \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A vertical screen begins at ground level \(30\,\mathrm m\) horizontally from launch and extends above the whole path. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Which does the ball hit first, and at what time?

retry.feedback: That is the later candidate. The assumed free flight ends at the first valid contact.

blocks.hint: Find both candidate times on the same clock and stop the free-flight equations at the earliest physical event.
blocks.solution:
The absolute height is \(Y=- 5 t^{2} + 5 t + \frac{75}{4}\). Ground contact has one positive time, \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\).

The screen's horizontal position would be reached at \(3\,\mathrm s\). Compare before substituting the final height.

The first event is the ground at \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm s\).

blocks.html: Solving one boundary equation in isolation can overlook a prior contact.

blocks.title: Compare two candidate first events
blocks.prompt: A ball is launched \(\frac{175}{4}\,\mathrm m\) above horizontal ground with rightwards speed \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and upwards speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A vertical screen begins at ground level \(48\,\mathrm m\) horizontally from launch and extends above the whole path. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Which does the ball hit first, and at what time?

retry.feedback: That is the later candidate. The assumed free flight ends at the first valid contact.

blocks.hint: Find both candidate times on the same clock and stop the free-flight equations at the earliest physical event.
blocks.solution:
The absolute height is \(Y=- 5 t^{2} + 5 t + \frac{175}{4}\). Ground contact has one positive time, \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\).

The screen's horizontal position would be reached at \(4\,\mathrm s\). Compare before substituting the final height.

The first event is the ground at \(\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\).

examples.title: Synchronise two airborne balls
examples.question: Ball A is thrown right from the origin with initial horizontal and upwards velocity components \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Ball B begins at the same time and level \(\frac{9}{2}\,\mathrm m\) to the right, with initial components \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time from A's launch to their meeting and its height above launch.
solution: Use clock time \(t\) for A and \(t\) for B.
Equating horizontal positions gives \(6 t=3 t + \frac{9}{2}\), so \(t=\frac{3}{2}\). At this time both balls have been launched.
Substitute each ball's own elapsed time into its vertical equation. Both heights equal \(\frac{63}{4}\,\mathrm m\). The meeting occurs \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm s\) after A launches.

examples.title: Synchronise two airborne balls

Choose the next step

SituationMethod
MeetingCheck both coordinates at the same common clock time.
DelayUse \(t-d\) for the motion that starts at time \(d\).
Smooth-floor impactKeep horizontal velocity and reverse and scale the vertical component.
ReleaseUse the actual tangent velocity at the release point.
First eventCompare all valid times before starting the next stage.

A ball hits a smooth floor with vertical velocity \(-12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(e=\frac34\). Find the new vertical velocity.
